intermediate_notes.title: Scaled Dot-Product Self-Attention Mechanics
intermediate_notes.author: Jay Alammar (The Illustrated Transformer)
intermediate_notes.math: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V
intermediate_notes.content: In self-attention, each input token embedding is projected into Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) representations via learned projection weight matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V in R^(d_model x d_k). The scaling factor sqrt(d_k) counteracts the growth of dot products in high dimensions; large dot products push the softmax activation into regions with vanishingly small gradients. After computing token alignments, multi-head attention concatenates independent attention heads and applies residual additions followed by Layer Normalization (LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))).

intermediate_notes.title: Lagrange Duality & Support Vector Machine Formulation
intermediate_notes.author: Andrew Ng (Stanford CS229 Notes)
intermediate_notes.math: max_alpha [ sum_i alpha_i - 0.5 * sum_i sum_j alpha_i * alpha_j * y_i * y_j * K(x_i, x_j) ] s.t. 0 <= alpha_i <= C
intermediate_notes.content: By formulating the maximum-margin hyperplane problem as a primal quadratic program with inequality constraints, we construct the Lagrangian L(w, b, alpha). Deriving the dual representation via KKT optimality conditions reveals that the weight vector w depends exclusively on the linear combination of support vectors (samples with alpha_i > 0). The inner product <x_i, x_j> can then be replaced by a Mercer kernel function K(x_i, x_j) = <phi(x_i), phi(x_j)> to project into infinite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces without materializing feature coordinates.

intermediate_notes.title: Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (Autograd Engine)
intermediate_notes.author: Andrej Karpathy (micrograd)
intermediate_notes.content: Modern deep learning frameworks construct dynamic directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) during the forward pass. Each scalar or tensor Value node records its operands and a backward closure implementing the local Jacobian-vector product. A reverse topological sort across the computational graph triggers .backward() in reverse execution order, propagating loss gradients dL/dw through backpropagation to update parameters: w = w - lr * grad.

intermediate_notes.title: The Geometry of Ordinary Least Squares (Hat Matrix Projection)
intermediate_notes.author: UC Berkeley DATA 100 Faculty
intermediate_notes.math: H = X * (X^T * X)^(-1) * X^T  ==>  y_hat = H * y
intermediate_notes.content: In multiple linear regression, the fitted response vector y_hat is the orthogonal projection of the observed response vector y onto the column space of the design matrix X (col(X)). Because the residual vector e = y - y_hat is orthogonal to every column in X, X^T(y - X*beta) = 0, which yields the normal equations: beta_hat = (X^T * X)^(-1) * X^T * y. The Hat Matrix H is idempotent (H^2 = H) and symmetric (H^T = H), confirming it acts as a true geometric orthogonal projector.

intermediate_notes.title: Production SQL Query Optimization: The 6 Operational Rules
intermediate_notes.author: Career Learning Vault Relational Architecture
intermediate_notes.math: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ...
intermediate_notes.content:
1. Projection Truncation: Explicitly name required columns; eliminate SELECT * to avoid unnecessary disk I/O and network payload transfer.
2. Predicate Pushdown: Apply filters in WHERE before joins and grouping, eliminating rows as early as possible rather than filtering with HAVING.
3. CTE Query Decomposition: Use Common Table Expressions (WITH clause) to structure complex multi-step queries into readable, logically partitioned sub-pipelines.
4. Join Efficiency: Favor INNER JOIN over OUTER JOIN patterns when allowable to minimize memory allocation in join hash tables.
5. Window Function Optimization: Use analytic window functions (ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), LEAD(), LAG()) with PARTITION BY to eliminate slow self-joins.
6. Execution Plan Diagnostics: Inspect EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE traces to detect sequential table scans and create appropriate B-Tree or Hash indexes.

intermediate_notes.title: Simpson's Paradox & Confounding Variables in Data Science
intermediate_notes.author: UC Berkeley Human Contexts and Ethics Group
intermediate_notes.math: P(A | B) > P(A | ~B) but P(A | B, C) < P(A | ~B, C)
intermediate_notes.content: Simpson's Paradox occurs when a statistical trend appears across distinct groups of data but disappears or reverses when the groups are aggregated. This happens when a confounding variable correlates with both the predictor and response. In production data pipelines, failing to stratify by confounding factors (e.g. user cohort, device type, geographic market) leads to false causal inferences and flawed A/B test interpretations.

intermediate_notes.title: Binary Memory Safety: Stack Layout, ASLR & ROP Gadgets
intermediate_notes.author: Nickolai Zeldovich (MIT 6.858 Notes)
intermediate_notes.math: Buffer Overflow -> Saved EIP / RIP Overwrite -> ROP Chain (pop rdi; ret)
intermediate_notes.content: Classic stack smashing corrupts the saved instruction pointer (Saved RIP) on the stack frame. Operating systems mitigated this using non-executable stacks (W^X / Data Execution Prevention) and Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR). Modern adversaries bypass W^X using Return-Oriented Programming (ROP): chaining existing short instruction sequences ending in 'ret' (gadgets) already present in executable code libraries (e.g. libc) to load registers and trigger mprotect() or execve() without injecting executable instructions.

intermediate_notes.title: OWASP Defensive Implementation Controls
intermediate_notes.author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
intermediate_notes.math: SELECT * FROM users WHERE user = ? AND pass_hash = ?
intermediate_notes.content:
1. SQL Injection: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) to structurally separate query syntax from untrusted client input. Avoid string concatenation.
2. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): Implement context-aware output encoding across HTML bodies, attributes, and script tags, reinforced by strict Content Security Policy (CSP) headers.
3. Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): Validate destination hostnames against an explicit domain allowlist, resolve DNS records to filter private IP ranges (RFC 1918), and block access to cloud metadata IP endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254).
4. Password Storage: Use salted adaptive password hashing algorithms (Argon2id, bcrypt, PBKDF2) configured with adequate memory and iteration work factors; avoid fast message digests like MD5 or SHA-256.

intermediate_notes.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 Architecture
intermediate_notes.author: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
intermediate_notes.math: Govern (GV) -> Identify (ID) -> Protect (PR) -> Detect (DE) -> Respond (RS) -> Recover (RC)
intermediate_notes.content:
NIST CSF 2.0 formalizes organizational cybersecurity into 6 core Functions:
- GOVERN (GV): Establish cybersecurity risk management strategy, organizational roles, policies, and supply chain oversight.
- IDENTIFY (ID): Determine cybersecurity risks to systems, people, assets, data, and capabilities.
- PROTECT (PR): Implement safeguards to ensure delivery of critical services (access control, data security, awareness).
- DETECT (DE): Find and analyze possible cybersecurity attacks and anomalies.
- RESPOND (RS): Take action regarding a detected cybersecurity incident (containment, mitigation, communication).
- RECOVER (RC): Restore assets and operations impacted by a cybersecurity incident.

intermediate_notes.title: The Operational Judging Server Rule (10^8 Operations / Second)
intermediate_notes.author: TakeUForward Operational Benchmarks
intermediate_notes.math: 10^8 basic operations ≈ 1.0 second CPU execution limit
intermediate_notes.content:
In online competitive programming and technical screening servers, a standard CPU executes roughly 10^8 basic operations per second. Given the problem constraint on input size N, you must determine your target Big-O complexity BEFORE writing any code:
- N <= 10: O(N!) or O(2^N) [Permutations, full backtracking]
- N <= 20: O(2^N) [Subsets, bitmask dynamic programming]
- N <= 1,000: O(N^2) [Nested loops, dense graph algorithms, Floyd-Warshall]
- N <= 100,000: O(N log N) [Sorting, divide-and-conquer, heaps, Fenwick/Segment trees]
- N <= 10,000,000: O(N) [Single-pass linear scans, two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums]
- N > 10,000,000: O(log N) or O(1) [Binary search, closed-form mathematical equations]

intermediate_notes.title: Hash Maps & Collision Resolution Strategies
intermediate_notes.author: TakeUForward DSA Compendium
intermediate_notes.content:
A hash table maps arbitrary keys to bucket indices using a hash function. When two distinct keys map to the same bucket index, collisions are resolved via:
1. Separate Chaining: Each bucket holds a singly linked list (or balanced Red-Black BST as in Java 8+ HashMap when bucket length > 8).
2. Open Addressing (Linear Probing, Quadratic Probing, Double Hashing): Stores all elements directly in the table array; on collision, systematically probes subsequent indices until an empty slot is located.
Load Factor (alpha = n / m): When the load factor exceeds a threshold (typically 0.75), the table dynamically rehashes into an array of double size to preserve O(1) average lookup time.

intermediate_notes.title: Algorithmic Correctness Proofs & Induction
intermediate_notes.author: Jeff Erickson (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)
intermediate_notes.math: Inductive Hypothesis: P(k) holds for all k < n ==> P(n) holds
intermediate_notes.content:
Jeff Erickson's 'Algorithms' establishes that writing recursive algorithms is mathematically identical to constructing formal inductive proofs:
- Base Case: Directly solve trivial instances of size 0 or 1.
- Inductive Step: Assume by induction that the algorithm correctly solves all strictly smaller subproblems; combine their results to solve the target problem of size n.
- Dynamic Programming: Analyze the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subproblem dependencies. A topological evaluation order ensures that when evaluating subproblem v, all dependent subproblems u in in-neighbors(v) have already been computed and stored in the memoization table.
